1000108.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Swahili Uganda (“Buganda, the kingdom”), from Luganda Buganda (“the place of the Ganda”). In the 19th century, Swahili traders rendered the name of the kingdom of Buganda as Uganda, a form subsequently adopted by the British. The name, originally referring to Buganda, was then extended to the larger territory under British rule and ultimately to the modern country.
Compare the parallel international adaptations Norwegian Nynorsk Uganda, Danish Uganda, Swedish Uganda, German Uganda, French Ouganda and English Uganda.

1001388.etyen:
Borrowed from Danish Bodil, ultimately from Old Norse Bóthildr, a female given name formed from bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) and hildr (“battle, fight”). The first element continues Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“improvement, betterment; recompense, atonement”), while the second continues Proto-Germanic *hildiz (“battle, fight”). The spelling Bodil entered Norwegian through Danish around 1900.
Related Norwegian forms include Bothild and Bodhild. Compare Icelandic Bóthildur (“female given name”).

1002668.etyen:
From Hans (“male given name”) + -ina (“feminine name-forming suffix”). The suffix -ina is a less common variant of -ine. Names of this type became fashionable in Norway in the 18th century, having been transmitted through Danish from German, and were chiefly used when daughters were named after male relatives. The base name Hans is a German short form of Johannes, which comes via Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs) from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”).
First attested in 1766 in Norway.
